blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a concerning study by Xing et al. on malvertising via browser extensions, revealing that 56 out of 292 Chrome extensions surveyed inject malicious ads through 16 ad networks, affecting over 600,000 users. The paper identifies three ad injection practices: injecting ads relevant to search terms, overlaying ads on retailer pages, and aggressively inserting ads across most web pages. The authors built a tool called Expector to analyze 18,030 Chrome extensions, finding 292 ad-injecting extensions with a low false positive rate. The study found that ad-injecting extensions serve a higher fraction of malicious ads compared to natural ads, with some ad networks serving exclusively malicious content, likely due to collusion or ownership by miscreants. The paper also explores the mechanics of malvertising, including redirection chains to drive-by-download landing pages and malware hosting domains, and shows temporal correlations between users resolving ad network and malware domains. Notably, some extensions abuse privileges to hijack user interactions, leading to malware downloads.
paper_title: Understanding malvertising through ad-injecting browser extensions
paper_abstract: Keywords Malvertising is a malicious activity that leverages advertising to distribute various forms of malware. Because advertising is the key revenue generator for numerous Internet companies, large ad networks, such as Google, Yahoo and Microsoft, invest a lot of effort to mitigate malicious ads from their ad networks. This drives adversaries to look for alternative methods to deploy malvertising. In this paper, we show that browser extensions that use ads as their monetization strategy often facilitate the deployment of malvertising. Moreover, while some extensions simply serve ads from ad networks that support malvertising, other extensions maliciously alter the content of visited webpages to force users into installing malware. To measure the extent of these behaviors we developed Expector, a system that automatically inspects and identifies browser extensions that inject ads, and then classifies these ads as malicious or benign based on their landing pages. Using Expector, we automatically inspected over 18,000 Chrome browser extensions. We found 292 extensions that inject ads, and detected 56 extensions that participate in malvertising using 16 different ad networks and with a total user base of 602,417. Malvertising; Browser Extension; Adware
